title: Kodak built a digital camera the size of a toaster.
description:
Kodak built a digital camera the size of a toaster. An engineer named Steven Sasson assembled it around a Fairchild CCD sensor. It weighed 3.6 kilograms.

It was 100 by 100 pixels, in black and white. That is 0.01 megapixels. The image was recorded onto a cassette tape.

The time it took to write one picture to tape. Capturing it took only 50 milliseconds.

You watched your photo on a television. A separate unit turned the tape data into a standard NTSC signal for a TV screen.

The executives did not see a market for it. Sasson told the New York Times they were convinced no one would ever want to look at their pictures on a television set. The camera was never produced.

Kodak invented it, then filed the patent and moved on.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Sasson: read. Established that Sasson, an electrical engineer, was assigned in 1975 to build an electronic camera around a commercially available CCD; the camera recorded 100 x 100 pixels (0.01 megapixels) in black and white from a Fairchild CCD, weighed 8 pounds (3.6 kg), took 23 seconds per image and recorded to cassette tape; Kodak filed the patent in 1977 naming Sasson and Gareth Lloyd (US 4,131,919).
- https://spectrum.ieee.org/first-digital-camera-history: read (IEEE Spectrum). Established that capture took 50 milliseconds but writing to tape took 23 seconds (Sasson's own words); that a separate playback unit converted the tape data to an NTSC signal for a television; that the device was about the size of a toaster; that Kodak executives said they did not see a market for it and it was never produced; and a patent granted in 1978.
- https://petapixel.com/2017/09/21/kodak-said-digital-photography-1975/: read. Established Sasson's account to the New York Times that the executives were convinced no one would ever want to look at their pictures on a television set.
